title: Choosing an Indicator
short: Choose an indicator whose color change falls on the steep part of the titration curve.
trouble: Students pick an indicator that changes color at pH 7 for every titration.

blocks.html: An indicator signals the end of a titration by changing color. Picking one means matching its color change to the steep part of the titration curve.

An indicator is a weak acid, HIn, whose acid and base forms have different colors. It changes color over roughly $\text{p}K_\text{In} \pm 1$. Choose one whose range falls on the vertical jump of the curve, which contains the equivalence point.

$\dfrac{[\mathrm{In^-}]}{[\mathrm{HIn}]} = 10^{\text{pH} - \text{p}K_\text{In}}$. Your eye sees a mixed color only while neither form outnumbers the other by more than about 10 to 1, so the change spans about 2 pH units around $\text{p}K_\text{In}$. On the steep part of a titration curve a single drop moves the pH by several units, so an indicator anywhere on that jump changes color within a drop of the equivalence point.

blocks.title: Weak acid, strong base
blocks.q: Acetic acid is titrated with NaOH; the equivalence point is at pH 8.72. Choose among methyl red, bromothymol blue and phenolphthalein.
steps: The jump runs from about pH 7 to 11.
Phenolphthalein (8.2–10.0) sits on the jump. Methyl red would change color long before equivalence, while the flask is still a buffer.

blocks.title: Weak base, strong acid
blocks.q: $0.100\ \text{M}$ $\mathrm{NH_3}$ is titrated with $0.100\ \text{M}$ HCl. At equivalence the flask holds $0.0500\ \text{M}$ $\mathrm{NH_4^+}$ ($K_a = 5.6 \times 10^{-10}$). Pick an indicator.
steps: Methyl red (4.4–6.2) brackets 5.28. Phenolphthalein would change color far too early, while the solution is still basic.

blocks.title: Reading an indicator constant
blocks.q: An indicator has $K_a = 1.0 \times 10^{-9}$. Around what pH does it change color?
steps: Its useful range is about 8 to 10, so it would suit a weak acid titrated with a strong base.

blocks.html: Choosing an indicator that changes at pH 7 for every titration. Only strong acid with strong base has its equivalence point at 7. Check: find the pH at equivalence first, then pick the indicator.
